narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 61% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was denied.

The three factors that mattered most in this decision were your LSAT score, your undergraduate GPA, and your first-year law school grades. Your LSAT score of 32 was the strongest influence and pushed the prediction toward failure; it sits well below the average of 37 among students who were accepted. Your undergraduate GPA of 2.70 was the second most important factor and also increased the likelihood of failure, falling noticeably short of the 3.23 average for admitted students. Your first-year law school performance worked in the opposite direction: being in the 6th decile was actually slightly helpful and nudged the prediction toward passing, matching the average of accepted students.

Taken together, the lower LSAT and college grades outweighed the positive signal from your first-year ranking, leading the model to conclude you were more likely than not to struggle with the bar exam.

What you should do next is focus on strengthening the areas the model flagged. Retaking the LSAT to raise your score, improving your study habits to lift your grades, or enrolling in a strong bar-preparation course could meaningfully change your profile for future applications. Many students improve these exact areas and go on to pass the bar successfully.
